stem.text: Lines 1 and 2 speak of 'such a commotion up and down a house'. What does 'commotion' on line 1 mean here?
quotes: such a commotion up and down a house

options.value: A great deal of noisy fuss.
A long argument between two people.
options.execution: There are cross words later, but line 1 is about the whole house being stirred up.

options.value: A slow and careful piece of work.
options.execution: A slow and careful piece of work is no meaning of 'commotion' and is close to its reverse. Lines 1 and 2 use the word for the whole house being stirred up whenever Uncle Podger takes on a job.

options.value: A crowd of people arriving at once.
options.execution: The child splits 'commotion' into parts she knows, 'com' and 'motion', and sums them into people moving in together. The parts are real but the sum is not the word: lines 1 and 2 mean a great deal of noisy fuss in the house.

options.execution: Invents a reason for standing there; line 26 says only that they are ready to help.

options.value: A tiny job has taken over the whole household.
The family were too busy to watch him properly.
options.execution: Lines 26 and 27 have the whole family standing round in a semi-circle, ready to help, which is the contrary of being too busy to watch. The child gives the family the opposite of what the lines show.

options.value: The picture is very heavy and needs several people.
options.execution: Nothing gives the picture a weight; the helpers hold the chair and pass small things.

rebuilds.why: Hold: stem and walkScript misquoted lines 27-29 as 'a second, a third...'; line 27 has 'Two people ... and a third'. stem.text: Lines 27 to 29 number the helpers: two, a third, a fourth, a fifth. Why does the writer number them like that?

options.value: To show the family were well organised.
options.execution: The child reads what the words say, that each helper is given a job, and takes it for good order. She misses what the count does: two, a third, a fourth, a fifth piles up people for one nail, and at lines 29 and 30 he drops it.

options.value: To show how long the job took to finish.
options.execution: Time is the business of other lines: half an hour is spent at line 24 and the picture is up about midnight at line 58. The child gives that effect to lines 27 to 29, where the numbers count people standing round at one moment.

options.value: To make the crowd grow bigger with every word.
To help the reader remember all their names.
options.execution: The helpers here are not named at all, only numbered.

explanationPatch.hintCore: Say the numbers in order. Ask what the counting does to the scene.
explanationPatch.walkScript: Look at lines 27 to 29. Two people hold the chair, then come a third, a fourth and a fifth. Each number adds one more body round the chair. The counting is what makes it feel like a crowd.

options.value: The charwoman's corns.
options.execution: The charwoman's corns are line 61, at the very end, when he steps off the chair on to them. The child answers from that later part of the passage instead of lines 43 to 45, where he slides on to the piano.

options.value: Somebody's toes, with a yell.
options.execution: True of line 48, but that is the hammer falling, not Uncle Podger. In the window, line 43 answers the stem: 'inches beyond what was possible for him to reach'.

explanationPatch.hintCore: Start at line 43, where the string slips. Read on until he stops sliding.

rebuilds.why: Hold: (1) 'He has learned... the job was hard' carried en-relation-word-flipped; the stored row already carries en-contradicted-by-the-text with an execution citing line 62's evident pride, which I checked and kept. Key reworded to 'He is as sure of himself at the end as he was at the start', which lines 6-7 (leave that to me, I'll do all that) and 61-63 (evident pride, some people would have had a man in) both support.

stem.text: Uncle Podger begins by telling them to leave it to him. He ends by saying some people would have had a man in. What does the writer show by this? (lines 6 and 7, and 61 to 63)

options.value: He has learned, as he did not know then, that the job was hard.
options.execution: Line 62 has him survey the mess with evident pride and say some people would have had a man in. The passage states the contrary of a lesson learned; he is as sure of himself at the end as at the start.

options.value: He is pleased, and glad they all helped so much at the end.
options.execution: Uncle Podger is proud at line 62, but his gladness at the family's help is what the passage denies: at line 37 he calls them all fools, and at line 52 he scolds the women for making a fuss. The child gives him gratitude the text states the contrary of.

options.value: He is as sure of himself at the end as he was at the start.
He is boasting to them, and hiding it, because it went so badly.
options.execution: A knowing reading, but line 62 states the pride as real, so nothing shows him aware.

rebuilds.why: Hold: walkScript cited line 1's 'always' (about Harris, not Uncle Podger) and claimed every action takes 'would' (false: line 57 'we had to find', 'a new hole was made'); and the 'remembered years after' distractor is arguably true of the retrospective narration. Walk rewritten: lines 1-2 set up what happened when he undertook a job, most of what he does takes 'would', with line 11 and line 37 as instances; 'would' declared as a quotation. Replaced the 'remembered years after' option with 'It tells us Uncle Podger was cross with everyone all day', tagged en-technique-intent-as-character (the writer's habitual 'would' read as the character's mood), which lines 61-62 (evident pride) rule out.

stem.text: The writer says 'would' again and again. He would shout, he would drop it, he would call us fools. What does that tell us about this day?

options.value: It is not one clear memory, but a guess at what may have happened.
options.execution: Takes the guessing sense of 'would', which the repeated pattern does not fix.

options.value: It tells us the picture was never hung, though he says it was.
options.execution: Stretches to never; line 58 has the picture up by midnight, crooked but up.

options.value: It tells us Uncle Podger was cross with everyone all day.
options.execution: The child reads the writer's choice as the character's state, so the repeated 'would' becomes Uncle Podger's mood. 'Would' marks what happened every time he took on a job, and he is not cross all day: at line 62 he surveys the mess with evident pride.

options.value: It is not one day at all, but what happened every single time.

explanationPatch.walkScript: Lines 1 and 2 set up what happened when he undertook to do a job. From line 3, most of what he does takes 'would'. He would shout at line 11 and would call us all fools at line 37. A single day would be told with plain past words, like shouted and dropped. So the passage gives what happened every time, not one day.

options.value: The house comes into sight.

options.value: The weather turns and the wood goes quiet.

explanationPatch.walkScript: Read line 8 and find the word suddenly, then count what follows it. Clouds, a stillness, silent rooks, the first rain. All four arrive together. The weather turns, and everything goes still and silent.

options.execution: Line 37 has Washington do it alone with a small stick, in a few moments.

rebuilds.why: Hold: walkScript paired 'charge it to her' with the stain, but line 48 answers her fainting; and lines 54-55 have the Otises reply directly that they are not afraid of ghosts, so 'every one belongs to running a house' and the key 'keep to household business' overstate. stem.text: Mrs Umney offers the family a ghost story. How do they keep answering it?

options.value: They keep saying, over and over, that the house has no ghost.
options.execution: Lines 54 and 55 have them say they are not afraid of ghosts. The child changes one detail, turning not being afraid of ghosts into there being no ghost, and matches the option on gist.

options.value: They laugh at her openly, while she is out of the room.
options.execution: Line 54 has them warmly assure her, and nothing anywhere has them laugh.

options.value: They never take her to heart, and answer her coldly.
options.execution: Line 54 has them answer her warmly, and line 57 leaves her better paid.

options.value: They mostly answer with everyday things, like stains, weather and pay.

explanationPatch.walkScript: Mrs Umney offers a murder, a ghost and a stain that cannot be removed. To the blood, Mrs Otis says it must be removed at once. Washington answers the stain with a stain remover. The thunder only gets a grumble about English weather. Her fainting gets a joke about charging her for it. At lines 54 and 55 they do say they are not afraid of ghosts. Even that ends in a pay rise for her, at lines 56 and 57.

Being lulled by the heat and dust.

rebuilds.why: Hold: the stem asked what riding inside stops her 'doing' while every option was a state, and lines 47-49 also show inside stops her checking her trunk, so the stem did not single out the window complaint. 'The stage is slippery and shiny down there' would now be a second key, so it becomes 'She wants to know what it costs to ride in front' (en-within-span-wrong-element: line 45 is a question, not a complaint). 'Her mother is very choice of the trunk' was true and mis-tagged, so it becomes 'The stage is far too small for her' (en-attribute-transfer: small belongs to the windows, line 47; the stage is too big, line 46). The trunk option is kept. hintCore and walkScript rewritten to the new question.

options.value: She rattles round, and she can only see bits of things.

explanationPatch.walkScript: Line 45 has her ask what it costs to ride up in front. That is a question, not a complaint. Lines 45 and 46 say it is slippery inside, and she rattles round. rebuilds.why: Hold: passageRef missing. Set stem.passageRef to stream-a-21-rebecca-sunnybrook; stem cites lines 57 to 59, lineRefs and executions were present. stem.text: Look at lines 57 to 59. What does Rebecca mean by a real passenger?

options.value: Somebody shut up in a coop like a hen.

options.value: Somebody with a long, long way to go.

options.value: Somebody who can see where she goes.
Somebody who has paid for a seat.

Line 58 gives the other side: down there she felt shut in like a hen. Down there, line 47 says, she could only see pieces of things. Up here she can see where she is going.

stem.text: Think about the whole passage. How much are we told about what Rebecca thinks?

options.value: She is shy at the start, but she is not shy by the end.
